descriptions.Part Number:
ST orderable part number: the unique ordering code that identifies the exact SKU.
Every row in the workbook is keyed on this value.
The full part number carries the package and temperature-grade suffixes in ST's naming scheme.
descriptions.General Description:
ST's one-paragraph marketing summary of the device, taken verbatim from the product page.
It positions the part in the portfolio, naming the target market and the headline differentiating features, and is prose rather than a structured field.
No data is derived from it; treat it as human-readable context.
descriptions.Marketing Status:
Commercial lifecycle state of the part at ST, for example Active (recommended for new designs), NRND (not recommended for new designs) or end-of-life/discontinued.
The status is ST's market classification and is independent of the datasheet's electrical claims.
It informs whether a new design should lock in on this part or prefer a successor.
descriptions.Package:
Package type(s) in which the part is offered, for example LQFP48, UFBGA, WLCSP or TFBGA.
One silicon die is often available in several packages with different pin counts and footprints.
The package name encodes the form factor, pin count and, on many parts, the body size.
descriptions.Core:
CPU core family of the device, e.g. Arm Cortex-M4, Arm Cortex-M7, or a dual Cortex-A/M combination on application processors.
The core together with its FPU and cache configuration largely defines the compute class and the instruction set of the part.
Dual-core parts show the primary core here; companion cores are described by Co-Processor type.
descriptions.Number of Cores nom:
Number of CPU cores integrated on the device (nominal): 1 for single-core parts, 2 for dual-core devices such as a Cortex-M7 + Cortex-M4 combination or a dual-Cortex-A application processor.
Dual-core parts apply the cores to asymmetric workloads, with the types shown in Core and Co-Processor type.
Nominal refers to the shipped configuration.
descriptions.L1 Cache (kB) typ:
Level-1 cache capacity in KiB (typical), normally split between an instruction cache and a data cache on Cortex-M7 and application-processor parts.
The L1 cache sits closest to the core and absorbs repeated memory accesses at full speed.
The reported figure is the combined instruction and data L1 capacity.
descriptions.L2 Cache (kB) typ:
Level-2 cache capacity in KiB (typical), a larger cache behind the L1 that serves the whole core memory system.
L2 is found on high-end parts (for example the 512 KiB L2 cache of the STM32H7 multimedia line).
Access to L2 is slower than L1 but faster than main SRAM or external memory.
descriptions.Operating Frequency (MHz):
Maximum CPU clock frequency in MHz that the device is qualified to run at.
Exceeding the rated frequency is outside the electrical specification and invalidates the published timing values.
The number reflects the highest speed grade of the given SKU.
descriptions.FPU:
Floating-point unit(s) present on the CPU, e.g. the single-precision VFPv4 hardware FPU found on most Cortex-M4/M33/M7 parts.
A hardware FPU executes float arithmetic in silicon instead of soft-float library emulation, which matters for DSP and control-loop throughput.
Blank means no hardware FPU; float is computed in software.
descriptions.Co-Processor type:
Type of the secondary processor core(s) embedded on the device, for example an Arm Cortex-M0+ or Cortex-M4 companion.
The co-processor runs independently of the main core and typically handles power management, radio protocol stacks, or a real-time watchdog role.
A blank value means the part is single-core or carries no companion.
descriptions.Co-Processor frequency (MHz) max:
Maximum clock frequency, in MHz, at which the secondary co-processor core can run.
The co-processor is a companion subsystem (for example a Cortex-M0+ or Cortex-M4) embedded to run low-power background, radio or real-time tasks alongside the main core.
The value is the co-processor's own ceiling; an application is normally clocked below it.
descriptions.DRAM support typ:
External DRAM families the memory controller can drive (relevant to application processors), for example LPDDR2, LPDDR3 and DDR3L under an integrated DRAM controller.
It states the interface families, not the maximum capacity or the number of memory banks.
Blank means the part exposes no external DRAM controller.
descriptions.Flash Support typ:
External Flash memory families the memory interface can address, for example NOR operated through FSMC/FMC or serial NOR through Quad/Octo-SPI.
Complement of DRAM support; it lists what external program/expanded storage the controller can reach.
This does not describe the embedded program Flash (see Flash Size).
descriptions.On-chip SRAM (kB) typ:
Embedded static RAM capacity in KiB (typical), totalled across the SRAM blocks the main core can address.
It excludes the core-coupled CCM regions tracked separately, and excludes cache memory.
This is the working-data memory available to firmware without external memory.
descriptions.Display controller:
Which display interfaces the part integrates, for example a parallel RGB LCD-TFT controller or a MIPI-DSI transmitter.
A built-in TFT controller drives a parallel-RGB panel directly; a DSI block carries the same frame data over a serial lane link to a display module. Both offload the CPU from the frame-refresh duty.
Blank indicates no display-driving hardware is integrated.
descriptions.Graphic accelerator:
Whether the part integrates a graphics processing block (2D engine, GPU, or display-composition accelerator, e.g. on application-processor parts).
An accelerator moves drawing, blending and compositing work off the CPU, which UI code benefits from directly.
This column is a presence marker; the exact feature set (chroma-key, rotation, blending) lives in the datasheet.
descriptions.Ethernet:
Ethernet capability of the part and its speed class, typically a single 10/100 Mbit/s Ethernet MAC.
An embedded MAC handles the media-access layer; designs still add an external PHY transceiver for the physical layer.
This column states capability rather than a connection count.
descriptions.Ethernet ports typ:
Number of Ethernet MAC ports the part integrates (typical).
Most devices carry a single 10/100 MAC; multiple-port parts are uncommon.
Blank means the part has no integrated Ethernet MAC.
descriptions.USB 2.0 typ:
Number of USB 2.0 interfaces on the device (typical).
USB 2.0 covers full-speed (12 Mbit/s) and high-speed (480 Mbit/s) device, host and OTG controller configurations.
The roles a specific part supports are detailed in the USB Type column.
descriptions.CAN (2.0):
Number of classic CAN 2.0B controllers (bxCAN) implemented on the device (typical).
The bxCAN block handles arbitration, message filtering and error handling for the Controller Area Network bus, and accepts both 2.0A (11-bit identifier) and 2.0B (29-bit identifier) frames.
Parts built around the newer FDCAN IP are counted under CAN (FD) instead, so a given part normally figures in only one of the two columns.
descriptions.CAN (FD):
Number of CAN-FD-capable controllers (FDCAN) on the device (typical).
CAN FD extends classic CAN with a variable bit-rate data phase (up to 8 Mbit/s in the data segment) and a stronger 32-bit CRC, while keeping the 1 Mbit/s arbitration phase of classic CAN.
A part with FDCAN still transmits classic 2.0 frames on the same bus; the two columns never double-count a single controller.
descriptions.I2C typ:
Number of I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) interfaces on the device (typical).
Each I2C peripheral is a multi-master two-wire (SCL/SDA) controller that can also act as a slave, driven over 400 kHz in most parts.
The count is of I2C peripherals, not of the individual busses they may serve at one time.
descriptions.I3C typ:
Number of I3C (Improved Inter-Integrated Circuit) interfaces on the device (typical).
I3C is the modernisation of I2C: backwards compatible, faster (up to 12.5 MHz), with hot-join and interrupt support that suits sensor hubs.
Each I3C peripheral provides one controller port plus slave capability.
descriptions.I2S typ:
Number of I2S (Inter-IC Sound) audio interfaces on the device (typical).
I2S carries stereo digital audio between the MCU and external audio codecs or digital microphones.
On parts where I2S re-uses SPI peripherals, ST still reports the usable audio links here.
descriptions.SPI typ:
Number of SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) ports on the device (typical).
Each SPI is a full-duplex synchronous serial controller, usually also usable in receiver-only or slave modes.
Some SPI instances are multiplexed with I2S; the audio capability is still counted where usable.
descriptions.USART typ:
Number of USART (synchronous + asynchronous serial) interfaces on the device (typical).
A USART adds a clock line and can operate in synchronous, smartcard, IrDA or LIN modes depending on the family.
The count covers the USART peripherals specifically, not the UART-only instances.
descriptions.UART typ:
Number of UART (asynchronous serial) interfaces on the device (typical).
A UART transfers bytes over a single wire pair (TX/RX) with no clock line.
USART peripherals that also provide UART mode are counted under USART, not here.
descriptions.Additional Interfaces:
Extra wired communication interfaces that the dedicated count columns (USART, UART, I2C, SPI and companions) do not already total.
This is the remainder of the connectivity fabric on top of the serial-peripheral counts, so treat it as a complement: blank here does not prove an interface is absent, only that ST's selector expresses nothing beyond the categorised sets.
The specific interfaces and their counts are what the datasheet's peripheral overview states for the part.
descriptions.External Memory Interfaces:
The external memory bus types the part exposes, for example a parallel FSMC/FMC controller, Quad-SPI, or Octo-SPI serial interface.
These let code or data execute from external NOR, NAND, PSRAM or DRAM mapped into the memory space.
The column lists interface families rather than pin or bus widths.
descriptions.A/D Converters 16-bit | Number of A/D Co:
Number of 16-bit analogue-to-digital converters on the device (typical count).
Sixteen-bit resolution is implemented as a sigma-delta converter on the parts that offer it, giving very high precision at lower sample rates than a fast SAR converter.
Only parts carrying a 16-bit converter populate this column.
descriptions.A/D Converters 16-bit | Number of Channe:
Total number of analogue input channels the 16-bit converter(s) can sample (typical).
As with the lower-resolution converters, the figure includes every input pin reachable through the input multiplexer.
Only parts integrating a 16-bit converter populate this column.
descriptions.A/D Converters 12-bit | Number of A/D Co:
Number of 12-bit analogue-to-digital converters (ADC) integrated on the device (typical count).
A 12-bit SAR (successive-approximation) converter is the standard ADC found on most STM32 parts; this figure counts the independent converter instances, not their input channels.
Several channels share one converter through an input multiplexer, so the converter count and the channel count (see the paired 'Number of Channels' column) are independent facts.
descriptions.A/D Converters 12-bit | Number of Channe:
Total number of analogue-capable input pins the 12-bit ADC(s) can sample (typical).
This counts every external channel across all 12-bit converter instances, including channels shared with other peripherals and the internal connections (reference voltage and temperature sensor).
A channel is a pin wired to the ADC input matrix, whether the application measures on it or not.
descriptions.D/A Converters (12-bit) typ:
Number of 12-bit digital-to-analogue converters (DAC) integrated on the device (typical).
The DAC turns a digital sample value into an analogue voltage on a dedicated output pin, commonly used for audio, waveform, or set-point generation.
Some parts integrate two independent channels; the figure counts converter instances.
descriptions.Timers (16-bit) typ:
Number of general-purpose 16-bit timers on the device (typical).
General-purpose timers provide timebases, output compare, input capture, PWM generation and simple encoder coupling.
Advanced and low-power timers are not counted here.
descriptions.Timers (32-bit) typ:
Number of general-purpose 32-bit timers on the device (typical).
32-bit timers are used where long timebases or high-resolution capture windows are needed.
Advanced and low-power timers are not counted here.
descriptions.Other timer functions:
Timer features that fall outside the counted 8/16/32-bit general-purpose set, listed by name (for example low-power timers, independent watchdogs, RTC alarm resources).
This is a capability list rather than a count.
It lets a designer see at a glance which specialised timing blocks a part carries.
descriptions.I/Os (High Current):
Number of general-purpose I/O pins rated for high sink/source current (typically the 20 mA drive class).
High-current GPIO pins can switch LEDs, relays or buzzer loads directly, avoiding an external buffer.
Only the high-drive pins of the given package are counted.
descriptions.Secure Boot spec:
Whether the part supports a secure-boot specification, for example a PSA (Platform Security Architecture) certified secure-boot implementation.
Secure boot cryptographically authenticates firmware before it executes, anchoring trust in an immutable root of trust.
It appears on secure/trusted product lines and is a presence marker.
descriptions.Cryptography:
Hardware cryptographic acceleration features of the device, normally a dedicated crypto processor supporting AES and, on parts that carry it, 3DES, SHA, HMAC and public-key arithmetic.
A hardware crypto block offloads encryption and hashing from the CPU and typically keeps key material outside ordinary application memory.
This column names the supported algorithms, not a count.
descriptions.Security Functions:
Security features beyond pure cryptography: secure storage, read protection, tamper detection, secure RTC, unique device identification and TrustZone-enabled isolation.
These capabilities support trusted boot, OTA integrity and anti-counterfeiting measures.
Cipher and hash algorithms themselves are listed under Cryptography instead.
descriptions.USB Type:
Which USB roles and speed classes the device supports, for example device, host, OTG, or DRD, and the corresponding interface type.
Roles determine whether the MCU behaves as a peripheral, masters the bus, or switches between the two.
The physical connector is chosen by the application; this column describes the controller's role set.
descriptions.Junction Temperature (°C) min:
Minimum junction temperature in degrees Celsius the silicon is qualified for.
Like the upper bound, the lower junction limit guarantees correct electrical behaviour down to this die temperature.
Together with the maximum it defines the full qualified die-temperature window.
descriptions.Junction Temperature (°C) max:
Maximum junction temperature in degrees Celsius the silicon is qualified to sustain.
Junction temperature (Tj) is the temperature of the die itself; it is driven by ambient temperature plus the part's own power dissipation.
The ambient operating range is stated separately under Operating Temperature.
descriptions.Supply Voltage (V) min:
Minimum supply voltage in volts the device requires to operate within specification.
Parts with internal regulators state the input-rail minimum; some families add footnoted lower limits (for example with the BOR detector disabled).
Where the datasheet qualifies the figure by condition, the selector keeps ST's published value.
descriptions.Supply Voltage (V) max:
Maximum supply voltage in volts that may be applied to the device's main VDD domain.
Operating above this ceiling is outside the electrical specification.
Where separate rails (VDDIO, VDDA or a radio supply) exist, the general figure may be narrowed by the most restrictive domain.
descriptions.NPU AI/NN Hardware Accelerator:
Whether the part integrates a neural-network / AI accelerator (NPU), found on AI-targeted lines.
An NPU executes quantised CNN and transformer workloads at far better performance-per-watt than the CPU alone.
This column is a presence marker; throughput and supported networks are specified in the datasheet.
descriptions.Video HW accelerator:
Whether the part integrates a dedicated video-processing block (for example an H.264 encoder/decoder on video application-processor parts).
A video accelerator offloads encode/decode and scaling from the CPU for camera and display pipelines.
The column is a presence marker; codec support details live in the datasheet.
descriptions.USB 3.0:
Number of USB 3.x interfaces on the part (relevant to application processors).
USB 3.0 / SuperSpeed provides a nominally 5 Gbit/s link where integrated.
Blank means the part is limited to USB 2.0 provision.
descriptions.PCIe type:
PCIe generation and lane configuration, for example Gen3 x1 or x2.
A higher generation doubles the per-lane bit rate, while more lanes scale the aggregate bandwidth.
Both determine the practical throughput the PCIe port can sustain.
descriptions.PCIe:
Number of PCI Express interfaces integrated on the part (relevant to application-processor parts).
A PCIe root port lets the processor attach high-speed peripherals, storage or accelerators.
Blank means the part exposes no PCIe controller.
descriptions.Longevity Commitment (yr) typ:
Duration, in years, that ST commits to keeping the part orderable, under the ST longevity programme (typically 10 or 15 years from launch).
The commitment is a supply guarantee window, not a projection of technical product lifetime.
Combine with Longevity Starting Date to know the guaranteed availability horizon.
descriptions.Longevity Starting Date:
The date from which the longevity commitment period begins to count (usually the product launch date).
Once a part moves toward end-of-life, availability is still guaranteed until this date plus the committed duration.
It is expressed as a calendar date in the product records.
